# Chapter 1: How do cyclical patterns impact avian functional diversity and niche structure ?

## Intro:

Laymans:

Biodiversity is not a static concept, and this where previous models that seek to understand how humans are impacting species, communities and ecosystems have fallen short. Functional diversity is a particularly informative dimension of biodiversity as, unlike species richness, it directly relates to ecosystem services. Different species have different functions such as seed dispersal, (e.g. pollinators), nutrient cycling (e.g. plants) and waste decomposition (e.g. fungi), and these functions impact carbon cycles, productivity and other crucial earth systems. Thus, at a given site the composition of species present, will effect ecosystem functioning. But, as day turns to night, seasons change and animals migrate and hibernate, species composition will change, and therefore the functional space will shift across time. Many of these functional shifts will be predictable, with cyclical patterns of species turnover.

For example, in the UK, a resident pigeon active during the daytime might help to clean up waste through scavenging. Whilst, a migratory nightjar, active at night might contribute to vital pest control but only during the months of April and May when it is present in the UK. If, under climate change, the night-jar's range shifts so that it no longer migrates to the UK during these months, this function may be lost entirely unless another functionally similar species can fill in the gap. Further, if species that are the most functionally unique and transient also happen to be the most climate-vulnerable, this would have severe consequences, particularly in areas where these species are most concentrated. 

By modelling how functional spaces change across time with species turnover and activity patterns, and how this is impacted by climate change, we can understand:
1. How climate change will impact ecosystem services
2. Which sites, seasons, time periods and groups will be most vulnerable to climate change (i.e. experience the greatest functional diversity loss/ loss of functionally unique species compared to present day)
3. How we can a) mitigate the impacts of climate change to prevent ecosystem degradation by either preventing climate change altogether and thus range shifts, or by targeting conservation efforts towards the most vulnerable species, groups and ecosystems in critical windows. Or b), more sub-optimally, how we can adapt to climate change under range shifts, by introducing new species/ re-introducing locally extinct species to fulfill keystone functions lost.

overlap of full AVONET space with AVONET beak space and non-beakspace against PC1 vs PC2 and PC2 vs PC3

Interpretation:
If AVONET beakspace differs to AVONET non-beakspace, suggests trophic trait space differs to non-trophic space (e.g. locomotion) so full trait space is needed to characterise the full diversity of avian functions
If beakspace/other space characterises the full trait space suggests only trophic traits (beak traits)/non-trophic traits needed

Interpretation:


PC1: Seems to represent overall size in all trait spaces with all traits having quite equal loadings i.e. large and long bodied/beaked species fall at higher values on PC1
PC2: HWI and tail length have strong influence in both full and other trait space, especially HWI. Species with high HWI fall at higher levels of PC2 i.e. migrants for full and other trait space respectively. In beakspace, beak length and width have strongest influence i.e. long-beaked species fall at higher values of PC2.
PC3: In full trait space, beak length and tail length seem to have strongest influence. Species with short beak and long tail fall at higher values of PC3. Same for other trait space, with short tarsus length replacing beak length. In beakspace, beak width and mass have strongest influence i.e. small, wide-beaked species fall at highest values of PC3.
PC4:In full trait space, narrow-beaked, species fall at high values of PC4. In other trait space, small bodied species with short tarsus length fall at high values. In beak space, wide but shallow-beaked species have fall at high values of PC4.

Migrants vs residents:

In PC1 V 2: Hand wing index has strong influence on other and full trait space with migrants with a larger hand wing index falling at higher and lower values of Pc1 respectively and other a full trait spaces thus seem to mirror eachother quite well.
removing that trait is seems there would likely be less inconsistency between beakspace and other pcs however, seems to be important for migratory status. - could remove as in (keyser et al., 2024) etc
In beakspace residents vs migrants seem to be seperated more by larger beak depths?

In PC1 v 3: trait spaces seem to be more similar 

In PC2 V 3: Trait spaces differ again but all three show clustering of residents vs migrants. Migrants = larger wing length and HWI for full space but not for other trait space where they are only seperated by HWI. Beak space more seperated by mass, i.e. large species tend to be migrants and occupy low values of PC3.

Next steps: remove HWI and kipps distance and see if traitspaces more similar (Keyser et al., 2024). Also wing traits likely highly correlated with kipps distance etc.

### Chapter 1. Exploring the temporal structure of the avian functional trait space using dispRity.

#loading in the data

```{r loading in the data}
mon_presence<- readRDS("~/Desktop/Phd Prep/Outputs/monthly_presence_by_site.rds") #species per 3kmx3km pixel per month

```

Analysis

## A) Testing seasonal patterns on a small scale (Britain and Ireland) with selected and justified trait space

### Preparing the data for the gridcell analysis

Winter season is defined as September-February in line with BTO Winter Bird Survey. Breeding season is defined as April-June in line with BTO Winter Bird Survey. 


```{r, echo=FALSE, preparing data }

#defining seasonal presence

#define winter and breeding seasons
winter <- c("Sep", "Oct", "Nov", "Dec", "Jan", "Feb")
breeding<- c("Apr", "May", "Jun") #change to summer?

#summarise seasonal presence of each species
presence.by.season <- function(data, seasons, groups = c("cell", "lon", "lat", "species", "local_status")) {
  flags <- imap(seasons, ~ expr(if_else(any(month %in% !!.x), "1", "0")))
  names(flags) <- paste0("present_", names(seasons)) #note that species present in at least 1 month in these seasons will be included in the seasonal trait space so doesn't distinguish between short-stay seasonal migrants and full-season migrants.

  data %>%
    group_by(across(all_of(groups))) %>%
    summarise(present_ever = "1", !!!flags, .groups = "drop")
}

mon_presence2 <- presence.by.season(
  mon_presence,
  seasons = list(winter = winter, breeding = breeding)
)

mon_presence2 <- mon_presence2 %>%
  mutate(across(c(present_winter, present_breeding), ~ as.integer(.x)))


#find species not present in either season at any site but present out of season
out_of_seasons <- mon_presence2 %>%
  group_by(species) %>%
  filter(sum(present_winter) == 0, sum(present_breeding) == 0) %>%
  distinct(species) %>%
  pull(species) # none!- means comparing to annual trait space won't work?

#how many species will be in the full seasonal traitspace? #useful for positional change in residents between seasons later on
n_distinct(mon_presence2$species[mon_presence2$present_winter == 1]) #226 species
n_distinct(mon_presence2$species[mon_presence2$present_breeding == 1]) #253 species

#11 migrant species present in winter season not present in breeding season these will be key to the niche switching in question 2 as will change the centroid of trait space across seasons.
setdiff(mon_presence2$species[mon_presence2$present_winter == 1], mon_presence2$species[mon_presence2$present_breeding == 1]) 

#38 migrant species present in breeding season not present in winter season, these will be key to the niche switching in question 2 as will change the centroid of trait space across seasons.
setdiff(mon_presence2$species[mon_presence2$present_breeding == 1],
        mon_presence2$species[mon_presence2$present_winter == 1])


write.csv(mon_presence2, "~/Desktop/Phd Prep/Outputs/species_site_season_df.csv") 

```

Using dispRity as opposed to mFD (Magneville et al., 2022) which relies on convex hulls that can be sensitive to outliers and insensitive to non-homogenous density distribution and funspace which seems only to handle two dimensional trait spaces and relies on TPD? (Carmona et al., 2024).

#Testing new metrics based on disprity vignette and shifting spaces Guillerme et al. (2020) paper

#Question 1: functional uniqueness: Do seasonal influxes of species introduce unique functions into trait space and therefore should we be taking account of cyclical change in functional diversity studies?--------------------

The inference would be that ecosystem functioning is dependent on these cyclical influxes
I.e. do migrants (cyclical species) contribute unique functions compared to the annual trait space and the resident trait space (year-round species) and does this change across seasons (winter vs breeding)?

#Mechanism: cyclical change (seasonal)
process: niche differentation (If they contribute unique functions (little niche overlap) then seasonal influxes of birds maybe key to ecosystem functioning but also this might be driving co-existence across the annual cycle (limiting similarity hypothesis). Alternatively if migrants do not contribute unique functions, and instead their niches overlap, then maybe migrants aren't so key to ecosystem functioning but also temporal partitioning may allow species to co-exist in the same niche (i.e. only when resources have peaked and there is enough to go around, might migrants be able to co-exist with residents). 

#i) Do migrants and residents overlap within annual trait space? (pairwise comparisons between groups) I.e. do migrants contribute unique functions to the annual trait space?- probabalistic hypervolume, ellipsoid volumes?-------------


(New) Metric 1a: hypervolume overlap ratio between groups (convex hull or probabilistic hypervolume around each group)?
- Non-overlapping volume/overlapping volume, larger = less overlap. 
- ses-controlled (draw random migrant and resident species from full annual species pool and quantify same ratio; does each site/ecoregion differ from what would expected by chance?)
- ses = observed value- mean value/SD, positive = less overlap than expected by chance, negative = more overlap.

#Plotting basic overlap between groups (ecoregions: migrants in each season vs residents vs annual trait space) in 2D trait space:
#a) Convex hulls capture size- sensitive to outliers
#2)ellipsoid and distance between and two group centroids- more sensitive to group orientation in trait space?

```{r}

 #load in species' seasonal presence by ecoregion
seasonal_presence_eco<- readRDS("~/Desktop/Phd Prep/Outputs/seasonal_ecoregion_pools.rds")



#load in trait space
avospace<- read.csv("~/Desktop/Phd Prep/Outputs/full_pca_scores_plus_status_nine_traits.csv")

#join pca data to ecoregional status and season data
avospace <- avospace %>%
  filter(species != "Upupa_epops") %>%
  select(-mig_status) %>%
  left_join(seasonal_presence_eco, by = "species")

#plotting by ecoregion- doesn't seem to differentiate that well
plot_eco<- 
  ggplot(avospace, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = ecoregion)) +
  theme_light()
plot_eco
```

#Metric 1b: distance between group centroids of seasonal migrants and resident commnuity in each ecoregion (testing uniqueness of migrant group again using a distance matrix); probably more sensitive to positional changes.

PERMANOVA: do distance between centroids differ between migrants (seasonal) and resident group (year round) within each season and ecoregion so do seasonal migrants contribute (ON AVERAGE) functions that differ from the resident community?

adonis2() tests whether group centroids differ in trait space

# BUT is this driven by heterogeneity of group variance (i.e. must factor in within group distance to group centroid)?

betadisper()  and permutest() tests whether dispersion is similar between groups (if not, then difference between groups more likely to be driven by spread (compare with SOV results) than position, will inform future metrics) 

```{r}

#ecoregionalx seasonalx migratory status presence
seasonal_presence_eco<- readRDS("~/Desktop/Phd Prep/Outputs/seasonal_ecoregion_pools.rds")

#9-dimensional avonet trait space
pc_avo<- read.csv("~/Desktop/Phd Prep/Outputs/full_pca_scores_plus_status_nine_traits.csv")

#join species seasonal and status data by ecoregion to pc scores
eco_pcs<- pc_avo %>%
  filter(species != "Upupa_epops") %>% #will need to recompute pca with traits for this species removed in future
  select(-mig_status) %>%
 select(species, starts_with(paste0("PC"))) %>%
  left_join(seasonal_presence_eco, by = "species")

#create pc matrix for distance matrix
avospace_mat<- pc_avo %>%
column_to_rownames("species") %>%
as.matrix()

#loop for calculating distance matrix on each ecoregion for each season
k <- 4 #4-dimensions for distance matrix #repeat on 9 to see if resukts hold
perm_result <- eco_pcs %>%
  group_by(ecoregion, season) %>%
  group_split() %>%
  map_dfr(function(assemblage) {
    if (n_distinct(assemblage$status) < 2 || min(table(assemblage$status)) < 4) return(NULL) #ensure all assemblages have at least two statuses and all ecoregions have at least 4 species
    d <- vegdist(assemblage[paste0("PC", 1:k)], method = "euclidean") #restrict distance matrix to 4 dimensions
    a <- adonis2(d ~ status, data = assemblage, permutations = 9999) #group distance to centroids
    b <- permutest(betadisper(d, assemblage$status), permutations = 9999) #controls for heterogeneity of variance between groups (i.e. spread within groups (within group distance to group centroid) needs to be homogenous)
    #return results in a table
    tibble(ecoregion = assemblage$ecoregion[1], season = assemblage$season[1], n = nrow(assemblage),
           R2 = a$R2[1], F_perm = a$F[1], p_perm = a$`Pr(>F)`[1], F_disp = b$tab$F[1], p_disp = b$tab$`Pr(>F)`[1]) #get R2 , F stat and pvalue from adonis2 and get F stat and dispersion p value from multivariate Levene's test 
  }) %>%
  mutate(p_adj = p.adjust(p_perm, "holm")) #only 20 pairwise comparisons so don't need BH but holm less conservative than bonferri


#plot variance within groups (betadisp)
disp_df <- eco_pcs %>%
  group_by(ecoregion, season) %>%
  group_split() %>%
  map_dfr(function(assemblage) {
    if (n_distinct(assemblage$status) < 2 || min(table(assemblage$status)) < 4) return(NULL)
    d  <- vegdist(assemblage[paste0("PC", 1:k)], method = "euclidean")
    bd <- betadisper(d, assemblage$status)
    tibble(ecoregion = assemblage$ecoregion[1], season = assemblage$season[1],
           species = assemblage$species, status = assemblage$status,
           dist_centroid = bd$distances)
  })

disp_boxplot<- ggplot(disp_df, aes(status, dist_centroid, fill = status)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.size = 0.8) +
  facet_grid(season ~ ecoregion) +
  labs(y = "Distance to group centroid", x = NULL) +
  theme_light() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

#residents more dispersed than migrants across all ecoregions and seasons, also tracks with sum of variances findings!

ggsave("box_plot_PERMANOVA_within_group_centroid_dist.png", plot = disp_boxplot, dpi=300)
```

Results:

- Distances between group centroids for migrants and residents vary in summer for celtic broadleaf forests, caledon conifer forests, english lowland beech forests and north atlantic moist mixed forests ,  in spring for caledon conifer forests and north atlantic moist mixed forests ,  and in autumn and winter for european atlantic mixed forests (p<0.05). However effect sizes are low, ranging from R2 = 0.0062 in Caledon conifer forests in autumn to R2 = 0.055 in north atlantic moist mixed forests in summer.
- Apart from english lowlands beech forests in summer (take group difference above with pinch of salt for this ecoregion), p values for the permutation test are above 0.05 suggesting homogeneity of variance between groups which is good. Residents are also more dispersed than migrants for all ecoregions and sites which tracks with sum of variances findings i.e. that residents are more spread than migrants.- confirm with ses distance to centroids with disprity?
- However, when performing holm correction, turns out that result is only significant for Caledon conifer forests and north atlantic moist mixed forests in summer (p=<0.05)
- results are pretty much exactly the same when rerunning on 9 dimensions
-with BH correction, more results are significant (p<0.05): caledon conifer forests, celtic broadleaf forests, english lowland beech forests, north atlantic beech forests in summer, and european atlantic mixed forests in autumn. But overall, suggests across most ecoregions that summer migrants are probably contributing the most unique trait combinations compared to the resident community.

#gridcells

```{r, testing new metrics with disprity}


  #seasonal presence of all species at each site (assemblage)
  site_seasonal_presence_df<- read.csv("~/Desktop/Phd Prep/Outputs/species_site_season_df.csv")
    
  #reading in raw trait space (not by site) 
  annual_trait_space<- read.csv("~/Desktop/Phd Prep/Outputs/full_pca_scores_plus_status.csv") #means of 9 species traits from AVONET (minus HWI and kipps distance) which are likely correlated and seem to skew trait space, also emulates (Keyser et al., 2024; for example)
  
  #converting to matrix for selecting axes
 annual_traitspace_mat <- annual_trait_space %>% #but maybe don't need to compare to annual traitspace as no out of season species? Ask thomas.
  column_to_rownames("species") %>%
  select(starts_with("PC")) %>%
  as.matrix()
 
#get row numbers of  winter and breeding species to feed into seperate lists so can calculate dimensions for winter vs summer breeding traitspace seperately. Will also be useful for full seasonal trait spaces needed in analysis 2 (resident positional shifting).
 
sp_seasonal <- list(winter   = unique(site_seasonal_presence_df$species[site_seasonal_presence_df$present_winter == "1"]), breeding = unique(site_seasonal_presence_df$species[site_seasonal_presence_df$present_breeding == "1"]))

 season_idx <- lapply(sp_seasonal, \(seaso) which(rownames(annual_traitspace_mat) %in% seaso))
 
 #annual vs winter vs breeding trait space variance
 selected_season<- select.axes(annual_traitspace_mat, group = season_idx, threshold = 0.95)
 #4 dimensions needed to explain 95% of variance in all seasonal groups
 
 selected_season$dimensions

#visualise variance of migrant trait space vs resident trait space vs whole trait space in plot
plot(selected_season) #all trait spaces seem to be vary similar in terms of variance


#migrant vs resident vs annual trait space variance
sp_mig_status <- list(migrant   = unique(site_seasonal_presence_df$species[site_seasonal_presence_df$local_status == "migrant"]), resident = unique(site_seasonal_presence_df$species[site_seasonal_presence_df$local_status == "resident"]))

mig_idx <- lapply(sp_mig_status, \(mig_group) which(rownames(annual_traitspace_mat) %in% mig_group))

selected_mig <- select.axes(annual_traitspace_mat, group = mig_idx, threshold = 0.95)
#4 dimensions needed to explain 95% of variance in migratory status groups (not sure if need to do this per site-level traitspaces but would take a lot of computational power?)

selected_mig$dimensions

#visualise variance of migrant trait space vs resident trait space vs whole trait space in plot
plot(selected_mig) #all trait spaces seem to be vary similar in terms of variance
 
 #do I need a trait space boundary i.e. controlling which points are allowed to fall inside the traitspace? apparently v 0.01 or 0.001 (conservative v value) is good for most cases (Carvalho and Cardoseo, 2025).



site.disp <- function(gridcell_rows, season, space = annual_traitspace_mat, axes = paste0("PC", 1:4)) {
  traits_per_cell <- space[gridcell_rows$species, axes, drop = FALSE] #get PCs for each species in each grid cell and convert to matrix (elements as rownames, PCs as columns)
  in_season <- gridcell_rows[[season]] == 1 #get grid cells per season
  groups <- list(annual   = gridcell_rows$species,
                 resident = gridcell_rows$species[in_season & gridcell_rows$local_status == "resident"],
                 migrant  = gridcell_rows$species[in_season & gridcell_rows$local_status == "migrant"]) #define migrant, resident and annual group
  groups <- groups[lengths(groups) > 3] #need at least three species in each group for calculation
  summary(dispRity(custom.subsets(traits_per_cell, group = groups), metric = c(sum, variances)))[, c("subsets", "n", "obs")]
} #calculate disprity metric for each grid cell trait space. Pairwise metric will be calculated between groups (annual vs migrant, annual vs resident and resident vs migrant) if between.groups = TRUE- will need for uniqueness metric.

#N.B. for species that have resident populations at some sites and migrant populations at others (partial migrants), their trait combinations will be the same in both bubbles so will contribute redundant functions. So in a way, the uniqueness of the group, may be a reflection of a lower number of partial migrants at the site.


result <- lapply(c(breeding = "present_breeding", winter = "present_winter"), function(season)
split(site_seasonal_presence_df, site_seasonal_presence_df$cell) %>%
    lapply(site.disp, season = season) |> #perform calculations per site for the breeding and winter seasons
    bind_rows(.id = "cell")
) |> bind_rows(.id = "season")

#create summary table of mean sum of variance per group (resident, annual, migrant) and season
result_table <- result %>%
  group_by(season, group = subsets) %>%
  summarise(mean_sum_var = mean(obs, na.rm = TRUE), 
            sd = sd(obs, na.rm = TRUE),
            mean_n_spp = mean(n), #calculate mean species per migrant group and season
            n_cells = n(), #number of grid cells in each group
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)


winter_season<- test.dispRity(result_table[mean_sum_var], test = t.test)
winter_season<- test.dispRity(mean(groups[breeding]), test = t.test)
    
```

Results:

- All cells included in calculations, minimum species number = 4, max = 182
- Weirdly, for both seasons, resident species tend to occupy more of the annual trait space/ be more spread out than all species (annual trait space)?.
- In both seasons migrant species tend to occupy less of the annual trait space than residents/be less spread (e.g. Hughes et al., 2022) (to be expected as likely a product of species richness).- but suggests migrants represent a lower diversity of functions.
- Breeding migrants occupy less of the annual trait space than winter migrants in annual trait space, but likely a product of species richness- will need to control for this (ses).

```{r}
#----------Disparity per ecoregion, status group and season----------#

#function calculate disprity calculations per status group, ecoregion and season using 4-dimensional space
eco.disp <- function(eco_rows, season, space = avospace, axes = paste0("PC", 1:4)) {
  annual_species   <- unique(eco_rows$species) #all species in ecoregion (all migrants + residents)
  resident_species <- unique(eco_rows$species[eco_rows$status == "resident"]) #all resident species in ecoregion
#migrant species in each season in ecoregion
  migrant_species  <- unique(eco_rows$species[eco_rows$season == season & eco_rows$status == "migrant"])

 #create subsets (migrant vs resident vs annual trait space for each ecoregion). Annual and resident trait spaces will not differ across seasons, but will differ between ecoregions. So we are comparing the difference between each seasonal migrant group to the resident and annual (which includes migrants not present in the focal season) trait spaces in each ecoregion. I.e. the difference between resident and annual will be the same across every season so we are interested in how the migrant space differs.
groups <- list(annual = annual_species, resident = resident_species, migrant = migrant_species)
  groups <- groups[lengths(groups) > 3]  # need >= 4 species per group as same as number of dimensions and disp calcs need 3 elements
  if (length(groups) == 0) return(NULL)
  
#PC coords for all species in full annual ecoregional traitspace
traits_per_eco <- space[annual_species, axes, drop = FALSE]

#calculate sum of variances per status group, season, and ecoregion
summary(dispRity(custom.subsets(traits_per_eco, group = groups),
                   metric = c(sum, variances)))[, c("subsets", "n", "obs")]
}

#define seasons
seasons <- c(spring = "Spring", summer = "Summer", autumn = "Autumn", winter = "Winter")

#apply disp calc to ecoregions in each season seperately
result <- lapply(seasons, function(season) {
  split(seasonal_presence_eco, seasonal_presence_eco$ecoregion) %>%
    lapply(eco.disp, season = season) %>%
    bind_rows(.id = "ecoregion")
}) %>%
  bind_rows(.id = "season")


#Pairwise metric will be calculated between groups (annual vs migrant, annual vs resident and resident vs migrant) if between.groups = TRUE- will need for uniqueness metric.

#remember that partial migrants are treated as residents to avoid redundancy across trait spaces, otherwise differences may be due to a smaller proportion of partial migrants in the ecoregion.

#create summary table of mean sum of variance per group (resident, annual, migrant) and season across all ecoregions
mean_result <- result %>%
  group_by(season, group = subsets) %>%
  summarise(mean_sum_var = mean(obs, na.rm = TRUE),
            sd = sd(obs, na.rm = TRUE),
            mean_n_spp = mean(n), #calculate avg n. species per status group and season
            n_ecos = dplyr::n(),
            .groups = "drop") #number of eco_regions in each group to check that all calculations were successful
 
 knitr::kable(mean_result, digits = 3)


#summarise sum of variances per ecoregion and status group in each season
per_eco_result <- result %>%
  transmute(ecoregion, season, group = subsets, n_spp = n, sum_var = obs)

knitr::kable(per_eco_result, digits = 3)



#get list of species in trait space for species migratory status crosschecks
ecospace<- avospace %>%
as.data.frame() %>%
rownames_to_column("species") %>%
  pull(species)

writeLine(ecospace)


#next step- SES.

#other considerations = ellipsoid volume is sensitive to a small number of extreme points 


```


Results:

- All 5 ecoregions included in calculations. 
- Migrants groups have lower species richness than resident groups across all seasons and ecoregions except spring migrants in European Atlantic mixed forests where species richness is roughly equal to that of the resident community.- supports need for SES.  
- Migrants are less spread than residents and annual trait space across all seasons and ecoregions. This especially the case in summer (avg 15.2% smaller sum of variances), whilst, in spring migrants are more spread (avg 5.8% smaller sum of variances)- This may reflect the number of species (summer migrants = 62 species on average, spring migrants = 85 species on average). 
- Even where resident and migrant communities are roughly equal in species richness, migrants are less spread in the ecoregional annual trait space (good for local community analysis). Suggests residents encompass a greater diversity of traits and functions with potentially more extreme trait combinations, whilst migrants may be more clustered.



- So, although it seems that there is a lot of functional overlap with the resident community,there seems to be some non-overlapping parts of trait space that migrants are especially contributing to. 
- It also looks like summer migrants are less spread in trait space than residents (so seem to be less specialist/diverse) and  represent on average a slightly different trait composition (functions are not that redundant with resident community) (but this may be a product of the fact that a lot of migrant species are present in all seasons except for summer so summer is less functionally diverse).

#PERMANOVA on refined trait space

```{r}

#loop for calculating distance matrix on each ecoregion for each season
k <- 4 #4-dimensions for distance matrix #repeat on 9 to see if resukts hold
perm_result <- avospace %>%
  group_by(ecoregion, season) %>%
  group_split() %>%
  map_dfr(function(assemblage) {
    if (n_distinct(assemblage$status) < 2 || min(table(assemblage$status)) < 4) return(NULL) #ensure all assemblages have at least two statuses and all ecoregions have at least 4 species
    d <- vegdist(assemblage[paste0("PC", 1:k)], method = "euclidean") #restrict distance matrix to 4 dimensions
    a <- adonis2(d ~ status, data = assemblage, permutations = 9999) #group distance to centroids
    b <- permutest(betadisper(d, assemblage$status), permutations = 9999) #controls for heterogeneity of variance between groups (i.e. spread within groups (within group distance to group centroid) needs to be homogenous)
    #return results in a table
    tibble(ecoregion = assemblage$ecoregion[1], season = assemblage$season[1], n = nrow(assemblage),
           R2 = a$R2[1], F_perm = a$F[1], p_perm = a$`Pr(>F)`[1], F_disp = b$tab$F[1], p_disp = b$tab$`Pr(>F)`[1]) #get R2 , F stat and pvalue from adonis2 and get F stat and dispersion p value from multivariate Levene's test 
  }) %>%
  mutate(p_adj = p.adjust(p_perm, "holm")) #only 20 pairwise comparisons so don't need BH but holm less conservative than bonferri


#plot variance within groups (betadisp)
disp_df <- avospace %>%
  group_by(ecoregion, season) %>%
  group_split() %>%
  map_dfr(function(assemblage) {
    if (n_distinct(assemblage$status) < 2 || min(table(assemblage$status)) < 4) return(NULL)
    d  <- vegdist(assemblage[paste0("PC", 1:k)], method = "euclidean")
    bd <- betadisper(d, assemblage$status)
    tibble(ecoregion = assemblage$ecoregion[1], season = assemblage$season[1],
           species = assemblage$species, status = assemblage$status,
           dist_centroid = bd$distances)
  })

disp_boxplot<- ggplot(disp_df, aes(status, dist_centroid, fill = status)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.size = 0.8) +
  facet_grid(season ~ ecoregion) +
  labs(y = "Distance to group centroid", x = NULL) +
  theme_light() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

#residents more dispersed than migrants across all ecoregions and seasons, also tracks with sum of variances findings!

ggsave("box_plot_PERMANOVA_within_group_centroid_dist_aoh.png", plot = disp_boxplot, dpi=300)
```

Results:

Results have changed!- 
- permutation test reveals that migrant and resident group cetroids differ in Caledon celtic forests and North Atlantic moist forets in Summer (the only results to be significant after holm correction with unrefined trait spaces), and in Winter in Celtic broadleaf forets and English lowland beech forests and European Atlantic mixed forests, with small effect sizes (low variance explained, R2) ranging from 0.076 to 0.022.  
- further, in all ecoregions and seasons groups appear to have equal dispersion (among group distance to centroid) so this is good evidence that groups differ in centroid location, not just in spread. In general, for all ecoregions and seasons, residents are more spread than migrants, except for in european atlantic mixed forests (see box plot)
- However, after holm correction, migrant and resident groups differ in centroid position in european mixed atlantic forests in winter (p<0.05).

- for 9 dimensions, results are the same with only groups in european mixed atlantic forest differing significantly in trait space after holm correction. However, passage seasons (NA) in european atlantic forest also becomes signifcant (p<0.05) after perm test (but not after holm correction). Same results dispersion wise between groups.

- same results with BH (for 4 dims) except nothing is significant, with european atlantic forest groups in winter being just above threshold (p= 0.059). same results dispersion wise. Same results for 9 dimensions. This time european atleantic forests in NA season ("passage") also just significant (p= 0.047), but not after holm correction.

- SO overall european atlantic forest winter migrants seem to differ from residents (also tracks ellipse plots), and aoh proibably more accurate as better accounts for pelagic species which may have erroneous distribution mapped onto ecoregions if not accounted for. However, there are also not many distinct species in winter vs summer in each ecoregion i.e. many species are present in both seasons (mainly because to be counted as a winter or summer migrant, only have to be present in at least one month of that season), and there are more distinct winter than summer species so may be why winter is coming out as more unique.
- although european atlantic species only has 10 distinct species in summer so these may be particuarly functionally unique- should investigate this!
